Final Problem Statement: "The online learning platform is bleeding potential revenue, with a 60% non-completion rate and a reactive support system that identifies dropouts only after they have been inactive for 14 days—when re-engagement is nearly impossible. Although the platform possesses rich, time-stamped behavioral data (login velocity, video watch-time ratios, and quiz score volatility), this data is not leveraged for predictive intervention.  This project frames a supervised binary classification problem, targeting the early prediction (by Day 7 of enrollment) of students likely to drop out. The key challenges are: (1) engineering temporal features that capture decay in engagement, (2) handling imbalanced classes where completers are the minority, and (3) optimizing for recall to minimize missed at-risk students.  The project will culminate in a deployable probability score for each active student and a feature-importance report, enabling the platform to shift from a reactive to a proactive retention strategy. Success will be measured by achieving an F2-Score > 0.75 on the validation set and delivering actionable business rules (e.g., 'If quiz score drops by 20% in 3 days, send a personalized check-in email')."

This project aims to solve this by building a predictive classification model using student behavioral data (login frequency, video watch time, and quiz performance) and demographic data to identify at-risk students as early as Week 2 of the course. The project will deliver a ranked list of dropout drivers and a probability score for each active student, enabling the operations team to launch targeted email interventions. The model's success will be evaluated based on its Precision, Recall, and AUC, prioritizing the accurate identification of potential dropouts to minimize false alarms.

H1 — Early behavioral trajectory outperforms total activity The slope of engagement in week 1–2 predicts completion better than total logins. A student who starts strong and fades is higher risk than one who starts slow and accelerates. H2 — Social engagement predicts completion independently of content consumption A student with low watch time but active forum participation may complete at higher rates than a passive high-watch-time student, because social accountability compensates for lower content engagement. H3 — Course category moderates feature importance Quiz scores may be the strongest predictor in technical courses (gatekeeping progress), while social signals dominate in creative or professional development courses where assessment is softer. H4 — Dropout risk is highest at two natural "choke points" After week 1 (novelty wears off) and at the midpoint of the course (effort vs. reward re-evaluation). A time-aware model — or two separate models for each window — may outperform a single static predictor.
